title: A Tiny Red Dot Might Be a Baby Black Hole
summary:
Imagine the universe as a newborn, only 450 million years old, and picture a tiny, fiery-red speck glowing in it. That is what the James Webb Space Telescope has spotted.

The speck is called CW-LRD-z10. Astronomers think it might be one of the earliest black holes ever found. It may belong to a strange group nicknamed 'little red dots': small, very red objects wrapped in thick clouds of gas.

Scientists measured its redshift, a number that shows how far away it is: 10.36, meaning its light left when the universe was just 450 million years old. The team found it in a 2025 search.

The clues fit well. Its color is much redder in mid-infrared light, and its light shows a 'V-shaped' dip like other little red dots. Takumi Tanaka said no single clue proves it alone, but together they make a strong case.

Scientists are being careful. The study did not cover the part of the light that usually shows wide hydrogen lines. Roberto Maiolino, a professor at Cambridge, said it should be called a candidate for now.
why_it_matters: Learning about the first black holes helps us understand how the universe, and everything in it including us, began.

background_read: A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape it.
The James Webb Space Telescope is a powerful telescope in space that looks at very faraway light to see the early universe.
Astronomers study tiny red dots like CW-LRD-z10 because their color and light may show that a young black hole is hiding inside thick gas clouds.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope, including Takumi Tanaka and Roberto Maiolino.
WHAT: A tiny red speck called CW-LRD-z10 that might be one of the earliest black holes ever found.
WHERE: In the very early universe, when it was only 450 million years old.
WHY: Scientists want to learn how the first black holes formed, so they are checking the clues to see if this speck is really a young black hole.
